strengths: Novel framing that focuses on the visual encoder as a source of hallucination, complementing the more common LLM-decoding-side literature (VCD, OPERA).

Fairly comprehensive empirical evaluation across three LVLM families (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP, Qwen-VL) and multiple benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE on three datasets, MME hallucination subset and full set, GPT4o-aided LLaVA-Bench), with consistent gains over vanilla and prior training-free baselines in most settings.
Extensive ablations (module-wise ablation, alpha/beta/K/l sweeps) and qualitative visualizations/case studies that make the mechanism of each component reasonably interpretable.

The three proposed mechanisms (token re-weighting, token subtraction via noise, adversarial-attack contrastive decoding) are individually simple and map cleanly onto the three diagnosed problems (statistical bias, inherent bias, vulnerability), which aids clarity of exposition.
weaknesses: The claim of being 'the first to trace LVLM hallucinations to visual encoders' is overstated; the paper itself cites prior work on CLIP token overemphasis/attention sinks [9,14], adversarial fragility of CLIP-like encoders [25], and long-tail/imbalanced pretraining concept bias [27] — these already implicate the visual encoder, so the core diagnostic claims are largely a repackaging/extension of known phenomena rather than a new discovery.

The statistical-bias analysis (Fig. 2a) and inherent-bias analysis (Fig. 2b) are purely correlational (based on one model, LLaVA-1.5) and do not establish a causal link between encoder-level norm overemphasis/noise-response and downstream hallucination; no controlled intervention (e.g., directly suppressing high-norm tokens with a real query image and measuring effect independent of the proposed method) is shown to validate the diagnosis in isolation.

Token re-weighting relies on a caption generated by the same 'vanilla' LVLM whose hallucinations the method is trying to fix; the paper's justification that hallucinated objects 'fail to match any visual tokens with high similarity' is asserted without empirical verification (e.g., no ablation quantifying re-weighting robustness under captions with varying hallucination rates).

The 'training-free' framing is somewhat misleading in terms of computational cost: the method requires (a) an extra forward pass through the vanilla LVLM to get a caption, (b) K forward passes through the encoder for noise tokens (though pre-computable), and (c) a per-image gradient-based adversarial optimization loop through the encoder/text-encoder — this is test-time optimization, and Table 11 shows ~7.6x inference overhead versus vanilla, comparable to OPERA, undermining the 'efficient alternative' positioning claimed in the introduction relative to training-based methods.

Results are mixed for InstructBLIP: gains are consistently smaller and sometimes negligible or negative (e.g., Table 4 Count score 75.3 vs 75.0, POPE Random split where OPERA outperforms SHIELD), and the paper's explanation (Q-Former constraining visual feature usage) is not further investigated or mitigated, leaving open whether the method is broadly architecture-agnostic as claimed.

Baseline comparison is limited to two training-free methods (VCD, OPERA); no comparison to more recent or additional training-free/training-based hallucination-mitigation baselines, and no statistical significance testing (e.g., variance across seeds/samples) is reported despite modest sample sizes (500 images for CHAIR).

The method introduces four sensitive hyperparameters (alpha, beta, K, l) tuned via ablation on a single benchmark/model (LLaVA-1.5 CHAIR); it is unclear whether the same fixed values generalize well across the very different architectures tested, given the noted weaker performance on InstructBLIP.

GPT4o-aided evaluation, while informative, is a single-judge, LLM-based metric susceptible to known biases (verbosity, position, self-preference) and the paper does not perform any human-agreement validation of GPT4o's scoring.
